set.statement: In emergency-department, psychiatric-emergency and trauma-centre series and in case reports, seen only through two reviews (figures second-hand; the primary studies have not been read), acute methamphetamine toxicity presents with sympathomimetic and psychiatric features whose reported frequency varies several-fold between studies and settings. A narrative review describes the common features, from case reports, as agitation, dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension and rapid respiration; other features include shivering, dyspnoea, chest pain, hyperpyrexia and cardiac, hepatic or renal failure, with coma and seizures less frequent, and deaths in case reports are attributed most often to pulmonary oedema or congestion, cerebrovascular haemorrhage, ventricular fibrillation, acute cardiac failure or hyperpyrexia. For non-fatal presentations it gives agitation in about 20%, suicidal ideation in 6–12%, acute psychosis in 7–12%, rhabdomyolysis in up to 14% and seizures in 3–4%, from a few series, some of them of amphetamine, without denominators. A systematic review of 23 studies (searches 1990–2017; 17 from the USA, 7 of them from one centre) could not pool any clinical feature, because the studies measured them inconsistently; study by study it lists tachycardia in 42% and 85% and hypertension in 6.4% and 69% of presentations (two studies), acute coronary syndrome in 9 of 36 methamphetamine-positive patients with chest pain, psychosis in 12% (two studies) to 80% (60 people at a psychiatric emergency service), agitation in 13% to 48%, aggression in 18% to 50% and suicidal thoughts or behaviour in 6% to 50%, mostly without stated denominators. Neither review gives a case fatality among presentations or compares fatal with non-fatal cases, so whether higher body temperature predicts death among people who present is not established; the narrative review cites forensic studies suggesting that a significant and possibly greater proportion of methamphetamine-related deaths arise from accidents, suicide and homicide. One series of amphetamine-related presentations (Perth, 2005) is a source for both reviews, so they are not independent.
set.plain: Severe meth poisoning can look like a body in overdrive: agitation, wide pupils, a racing heart, high blood pressure and fast breathing. Less often there is very high body temperature, chest pain, seizures, muscle breakdown, or heart, liver or kidney failure, and some people die. This picture comes from two reviews of hospital emergency studies and case reports; we have not yet checked the original studies, and some of them concern amphetamine rather than meth. How often each sign appears differs a lot between studies and settings: a racing heart was found in 42 of 100 patients in one study and in 85 of 100 in another, and psychosis in 12 to 80 of 100. Neither review says how many patients die. One review notes that many meth-related deaths come from accidents, suicide and homicide. Whether high body temperature predicts death has not been studied in the sources we have read.
set.magnitude: Second-hand, mostly without denominators. Narrative review, non-fatal presentations: agitation about 20%, suicidal ideation 6–12%, acute psychosis 7–12%, rhabdomyolysis up to 14%, seizures 3–4%. Systematic review, study-level and not pooled: tachycardia 42% and 85%, hypertension 6.4% and 69% (two studies); acute coronary syndrome in 9 of 36 methamphetamine-positive patients with chest pain; psychosis 12% to 80%; agitation 13% to 48%; aggression 18% to 50%; suicidal thoughts or behaviour 6% to 50%. Not given by either review: case fatality among presentations, the proportion of deaths with other drugs detected, or any comparison of fatal with non-fatal cases.
set.population: people presenting to emergency departments, psychiatric emergency services or trauma centres with acute methamphetamine toxicity (in some series, amphetamine)
set.exposure: acute methamphetamine exposure (in some series, amphetamine or other stimulants)

grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: The primary case reports and series cannot be appraised through either review: the narrative review's sources are unappraised (editors' narrative-review checklist on its study card: high), and the systematic review, itself of critically low confidence on AMSTAR 2, rated 22 of its 23 mostly retrospective chart reviews at low risk without showing the ratings.

grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Study-level frequencies differ several-fold (tachycardia 42% against 85%, hypertension 6.4% against 69%, psychosis 12% to 80%), without stated denominators or common case definitions, and the differences are not explained.

grade.domains.indirectness.note: Second-hand through two reviews (METHODS §6.3); some cited series concern amphetamine rather than methamphetamine, and three studies in the systematic review counted cocaine or other stimulants.

set.grade.reasoning: Descriptive features from case reports and emergency chart reviews start low (relation 'describes', METHODS §6.1). The claim now rests on two reviews: a narrative review (Cruickshank & Dyer, 2009), used as a pointer, and a systematic review (Sibanda et al., 2019) that searched four databases but pooled no clinical feature and reports no deaths (AMSTAR 2 critically low on its study card). Risk of bias, one level: the primary studies cannot be appraised through either review. Inconsistency, one level: study-level frequencies differ several-fold without explanation. Indirectness, one level: second-hand, and partly about amphetamine or other stimulants. Certainty very low (the floor). The two reviews share at least one primary series (Gray et al., 2007, amphetamine-related presentations in Perth), so they are not independent. Status mixed: the features recur across series, but their frequencies are inconsistent. Any statement about how often a feature occurs, about case fatality or about what predicts death needs the primary series read and, for prognosis, studies that compare fatal with non-fatal cases.

evidence_add.locator: Results › Systematic review: Clinical characteristics associated with methamphetamine presentations › Cardiac complications, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence_add.extracted: Study-level cardiac findings in people presenting after methamphetamine use, not pooled: 9 (25%) of 36 methamphetamine-positive patients with chest pain had acute coronary syndrome (Turnipseed et al., 2003); mean systolic blood pressure 148 mm Hg (95% CI 144–152), diastolic 86 (83–89) and heart rate 116 per minute (97.3–134.7), with 3 episodes of ventricular tachycardia and 15 of cardiac ischaemia and no denominator given (Hawley et al., 2013); tachycardia in 42% and hypertension in 6.4% (Fatovich et al., 2012) against tachycardia in 85% and hypertension in 69% (Lan et al., 1998).

evidence_add.locator: Table 1, column 'Behaviour or presenting problem (%)' (pp. 5–6); Results › Systematic review › Behavioural and psychiatric problems, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 7)
evidence_add.extracted: Study-level psychiatric and behavioural findings, mostly without stated denominators: agitated delirium 20%, psychosis 12% and suicidal thoughts 6% among amphetamine-related presentations in Perth (Gray et al., 2007); psychotic 12% and suicidal 25% (Cloutier et al., 2013); aggression 18% (Bunting et al., 2007); suicide attempts 50% among 44 patients admitted for methamphetamine intoxication (Lan et al., 1998); psychosis 80%, suicidal 40% and agitation 13% (Pasic et al., 2007), in whose psychiatric emergency sample 48 of 60 methamphetamine-related presentations were acutely psychotic; aggression 50% and paranoia 86% (Szuster, 1990); agitation 48% and suicidal 47% (Toles et al., 2006).

evidence_add.locator: Methods › Selection criteria, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Results › Study characteristics, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 4); Table 1, Turnipseed et al. (2003) row (p. 6); Discussion › Critical reflection of the literature, 1st paragraph (p. 10, quotation)
evidence_add.extracted: The review could not pool any clinical feature: the studies had no consistent measures of clinical characteristics, so its meta-analyses were limited to sex, age and the share of methamphetamine-positive attendees. Chart reviews identified use, its pattern, the type of methamphetamine and other drug use poorly; three included studies counted cocaine or other stimulant use; positive urine toxicology likely includes other amphetamine-like compounds and stays positive for 72 hours; time of last use was not recorded. Two sets of included studies are linked to the same data, and Table 1 lists the acute coronary syndrome study with 171 subjects, against 36 in the text. No deaths or case fatality are reported anywhere in the review's results.
evidence_add.quote: no consistent measures of clinical characteristics across studies

change: First reader (AI reader 13) from the PDF of a systematic review (Sibanda et al., 2019; pp. 1–12): three anchors added (located), one with an 8-word quotation. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review: the statement, plain text, magnitude, population and exposure now add the systematic review's study-level frequencies (tachycardia 42% and 85%, hypertension 6.4% and 69%, psychosis 12% to 80%, agitation 13% to 48%, aggression 18% to 50%, suicidal thoughts or behaviour 6% to 50%; acute coronary syndrome in 9 of 36 chest-pain patients), which it could not pool, and say that neither review gives a case fatality and that the two reviews share a primary series. Inconsistency downgraded one level (frequencies differ several-fold without explanation); certainty unchanged (very low, the floor). Status single-study → mixed. Verification draft → metadata-verified: every anchor is located in a full text, both references are verified and retraction-checked, and the claim no longer rests only on narrative reviews (METHODS §6.3, §12).

set.statement: The US National Comorbidity Survey (1990–1992; household sample aged 15–54; structured CIDI interview) reported, for each drug class separately, the proportion of people who had ever used it who had ever met DSM-III-R criteria for dependence, with non-medical use of stimulants other than cocaine counted as one class. Among people who had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically (15.3% of the population; dextroamphetamine and methamphetamine are the examples given), 11.2% (SE 1.6; about 8.1% to 14.3%, editors' calculation) had ever met the criteria, against 31.9% for tobacco (no standard error; tobacco use came from a separate 1991 survey and dependence was assessed for daily smoking in a subsample), 15.4% for alcohol, 16.7% for cocaine, 23.1% for heroin and 9.1% for cannabis. Such proportions are taken at a single interview among everyone who had ever used, including once (the dependence questions were asked only of people reporting more than a few occasions of use), and do not account for people who started recently; the data are three decades old, grouped across stimulants and based on DSM-III-R criteria. The source calls the class psychostimulants other than cocaine; it includes extramedical use of prescription stimulants. A 2007 Australian national household survey (8,841 people aged 16–85; response 60%; WMH-CIDI 3.0 interview) measured something different. Its outcome was broader, DSM-IV stimulant abuse or dependence, in a stimulant class the paper does not define. Of 579 people who had used stimulants, 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8) had met the criteria by the interview. A survival analysis, which uses the years since each person first used and so allows for people who had started recently, estimated a cumulative probability of 50.4% (no interval given) of developing the disorder within 14 years of first use, 12.2% within the first year. The criteria were asked only of people who had used at least five times, and the authors note that counting abuse as well as dependence gives higher estimates than studies of dependence alone. The two surveys therefore measure different quantities and cannot be compared directly, and neither gives a figure for methamphetamine alone.
set.plain: A large US survey from the early 1990s counted, for each kind of drug, how many of the people who had ever used it had ever been dependent on it. About 11 in 100 of the people who had ever used stimulants other than cocaine (such as amphetamine or meth) without a prescription, or not as prescribed, had been dependent on them at some point, compared with about 32 in 100 for tobacco, 15 in 100 for alcohol and 17 in 100 for cocaine. That survey counted everyone who had ever tried a drug, even once, on the day of the interview, so people who had started only recently had had little time to become dependent. An Australian survey from 2007 asked a different question. It estimated how many of the people who had used stimulants (it does not say which ones) would develop dependence or a related diagnosis called abuse within 14 years of first using them: about 50 in 100, with about 46 in 100 already affected when they were interviewed. Because the two surveys measure different things, the higher Australian number does not show that the risk has gone up. Both surveys lump stimulants together, and neither gives a number for meth alone.
set.magnitude: US NCS (weighted, n = 8,098; Table 2): proportion ever dependent (DSM-III-R) among people who had ever used extramedically: psychostimulants other than cocaine 11.2% (SE 1.6; editors' 95% CI about 8.1% to 14.3%), from 15.3% lifetime use and 1.7% lifetime dependence in the population; tobacco 31.9% (no SE), alcohol 15.4% (0.7), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), cannabis 9.1% (0.7), heroin 23.1% (5.6). Stimulants by age: 13.5% (15–24), 13.9% (25–34), 7.7% (35–44), 6.5% (45–54); by sex: men 9.7%, women 13.3% (Tables 4–5). Australia 2007 (NSMHWB; weighted; stimulant class not defined; DSM-IV abuse or dependence): 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8) of 579 people who had used stimulants had ever met the criteria at interview; cumulative probability by years since first use (discrete-time survival analysis, no interval) 12.2% within the first year and 50.4% within 14 years; among those who developed the disorder, half did so within about 3 years (IQR 1–5) of first use.
set.population: US household (noninstitutionalized) population aged 15–54 in 1990–1992 who had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically; Australian household population aged 16–85 in 2007 who had ever used stimulants (class not defined)
set.exposure: lifetime extramedical use of psychostimulants other than cocaine, including prescription stimulants used without or beyond a prescription (US); lifetime use of stimulants, class not defined (Australia)
set.outcome: lifetime DSM-III-R dependence, as a proportion at interview (US); lifetime DSM-IV abuse or dependence, as a proportion at interview and as a cumulative probability by years since first use (Australia)

grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded for the US figures (JBI items met or largely met, study card overall low: national probability sample, response 82.4% with weighting, a standardized CIDI interview and design-based standard errors; frame, deaths and self-report could move the figure in either direction but not materially). Downgraded one level for the Australian figures (JBI moderate on the study card): response 60% with no non-response analysis reported, ages of first use and onset recalled at one interview and coded by inconsistent rules, and a denominator that may or may not include people who had used fewer than five times.

grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: the two surveys do not estimate the same quantity (outcome, measure, stimulant class, country and decade differ), so the gap between 11.2% and 45.7–50.4% is not heterogeneity in the GRADE sense; the statement presents the figures separately and says they cannot be compared.

grade.domains.indirectness.note: US: psychostimulants other than cocaine, of which methamphetamine is one example, including extramedical use of prescription stimulants; DSM-III-R; 1990–1992. Australia: a stimulant class that is not defined (it may include cocaine and other stimulants), an outcome that includes DSM-IV abuse; 2007. Neither gives a methamphetamine-specific figure.

set.grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (proportions and a cumulative probability in survey populations): starts low. Risk of bias, one level, for the Australian figures only (60% response, recalled timing, unclear denominator); the US figures are not downgraded (JBI low; the authors discuss frame, deaths and self-report, pp. 263–265). Indirectness, two levels: neither survey isolates methamphetamine, the US class includes extramedical use of prescription stimulants, and the Australian class is undefined and its outcome includes abuse; the criteria are DSM-III-R (1990–1992) and DSM-IV (2007). Not downgraded for inconsistency, because the two figures measure different things: a proportion ever dependent among everyone who had ever used, at one interview, against a projected cumulative probability of abuse or dependence by 14 years after first use. Certainty very low. The tobacco proportion is less comparable than the others: it combines tobacco use from a separate 1991 survey with dependence assessed for daily smoking in a subsample, and has no standard error. Status mixed: two surveys whose figures for stimulants are four- to five-fold apart, with candidate explanations (abuse counted, undefined class, a denominator that may exclude people with few uses, country and decade) that have not been tested. The US authors conclude from their figures that many, perhaps most, people who use a drug do not become dependent (p. 265); for stimulants, the Australian survival estimate (about half within 14 years, abuse included) shows that this conclusion depends on the measure and on how the outcome is defined.

evidence_add.locator: Methods › 2.1. Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, and 2.2. Measures, 1st paragraph (p. 137); Methods › 2.3. Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph, and Results › 3.2.1. Discrete Time Survival Analysis, 3rd paragraph (p. 138)
evidence_add.extracted: 2007 Australian National Survey of Mental Health and Wellbeing: 8,841 respondents aged 16–85 from a stratified multistage household probability sample, response 60%; lifetime DSM-IV abuse or dependence by a modified WMH-CIDI 3.0, with the criteria asked only of people who had used a drug at least five times. Of the 579 people who had used stimulants and gave a valid age of first use, 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8) had a lifetime stimulant use disorder at the interview (a descriptive conditional probability); median age of onset 20 years (IQR 18–24). The paper does not name the drugs in its stimulant class.

evidence_add.locator: Results › 3.2.1. Discrete Time Survival Analysis, 1st paragraph, and 3.3. Cumulative conditional probability and speed of transitioning to SUD among substance users, 1st paragraph (p. 138); Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 139)
evidence_add.extracted: Discrete-time survival analysis from first use, with people who had not developed the disorder censored at their age at interview and the stimulant data right-censored at 14 years after first use: cumulative probability of a stimulant use disorder 12.2% within the first year and 50.4% within an estimated 14 years, with no interval given; half of the stimulant cases had onset about 3 years (IQR 1–5) after first use. The authors state that these estimates are substantially higher than in other surveys, where the highest had been around one in four for cocaine, opioids and alcohol, and that studies counting dependence without abuse give lower estimates.

change: First reader (AI reader 13) from the PDF of an analysis of the 2007 Australian national mental-health survey (Marel et al., 2019; pp. 136–142): two qualifying anchors added (located). The statement, plain text, magnitude, population, exposure and outcome now add its figures for stimulants (45.7%, 95% CI 39.5–51.8, with a lifetime DSM-IV abuse or dependence at interview; cumulative probability 50.4% within 14 years of first use, 12.2% within the first year) and explain that this cumulative probability of developing a disorder over time, with abuse included, is a different measure from the US proportion ever dependent at one interview, so the two cannot be compared directly. Risk of bias downgraded one level for the Australian figures (60% response, recalled timing, unclear denominator); inconsistency not downgraded (different quantities); certainty unchanged (very low). Status single-study → mixed (two surveys, stimulant figures four- to five-fold apart, explanations untested).

set.statement: Whether amphetamine use (amphetamine or methamphetamine) is associated with violence after accounting for other factors is not settled. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, the pooled adjusted odds ratio was 1.4 (95% CI 0.8–2.4; 6 studies), against 2.2 (1.2–4.1; 10 studies, I² 95%) unadjusted. In unadjusted post hoc subgroups, violent behaviour (hostility rating scales, violent behaviour or sexual exploitation reported in surveys, and violent or self-destructive behaviour in an emergency department) was associated (3.7, 3.1–4.5) and violent offending was not clearly associated (1.0, 0.4–2.7; I² 94%). For amphetamine use disorder the review has a single study: among offenders whose punishment was reduced or waived because of mental disorder, those with the disorder had more violent re-offending over 7 years (unadjusted OR 6.2, 3.1–12.3; 52 people with the disorder; quality score 43%). The violence studies had among the lowest quality ratings in the review, with poor measurement of use; the review's authors judge that large effects in two population surveys and two longitudinal studies suggest that an association may exist but needs confirmation. The review also describes a within-person analysis of the same Australian treatment cohort as the psychosis study in section 9, in which severe hostility was more frequent during periods of use after adjustment for concurrent other drug use; that paper has not yet been read. A later general-population birth cohort, not in the review (Christchurch, New Zealand; about 1,000 people interviewed at 21, 25, 30 and 35; 28% used methamphetamine or amphetamine at least once between 18 and 35), found that use in a period went with more self-reported violence in the same period after adjustment for childhood and adolescent factors and for concurrent depression, anxiety, alcohol and cannabis use disorders, life stress, unemployment and psychotic symptoms: perpetration OR 1.60 (1.01–2.54), victimisation 1.57 (1.00–2.47), intimate-partner violence perpetration 1.55 (1.04–2.30) and victimisation 1.09 (0.80–1.49). Odds were higher among the 51 people who had used at least weekly (perpetration 4.84, 2.48–9.46), in an analysis adjusted for childhood factors only, while less frequent use was not clearly associated with perpetration (1.13 and 1.40, intervals including 1). Use and violence were reported for the same periods, so which came first is unknown, and other illicit drug use was not adjusted for.
set.plain: Is amphetamine use, including meth, linked to violence once other factors are taken into account? The evidence doesn't settle it. In a review of mostly weak studies, the link seen in raw numbers shrank and became uncertain after adjustment; it was seen for violent behaviour but not clearly for violent offences. A later study followed about 1,000 people in New Zealand from age 18 to 35. In periods when they used meth or speed, people were somewhat more likely to report attacking someone or being attacked, even after many other factors were taken into account, and more so among the few who used at least weekly. But use and violence were reported for the same years, so the study cannot show which came first, and it did not take other illegal drugs into account. One study that compared people with themselves found more hostility in periods of use; it has not been read yet. The review's authors think a link may exist but needs to be confirmed.
set.magnitude: Review (any use): adjusted OR 1.4 (0.8–2.4), 6 studies, I² 25%; unadjusted 2.2 (1.2–4.1), 10 studies, I² 95%; violent behaviour 3.7 (3.1–4.5); violent offending 1.0 (0.4–2.7). Birth cohort (any use in a period, fully adjusted): perpetration 1.60 (1.01–2.54), victimisation 1.57 (1.00–2.47), intimate-partner perpetration 1.55 (1.04–2.30), intimate-partner victimisation 1.09 (0.80–1.49); at least weekly use against never, adjusted for childhood factors only: perpetration 4.84 (2.48–9.46), victimisation 3.62 (1.88–6.96).
set.population: General-population (including a New Zealand birth cohort followed from 18 to 35), clinical and justice samples
set.exposure: Any amphetamine use (in the birth cohort, self-reported use of methamphetamine or amphetamine in each interview period)
set.outcome: Violent behaviour or violent offending (in the birth cohort, self-reported perpetration and victimisation, including intimate-partner violence)

grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: The review's violence studies had among the lowest quality scores (56–58%), with poor measurement of use. The birth cohort is stronger but at high risk of bias overall on its study card (ROBINS-E): use and violence reported for the same periods (reverse causation possible), self-reported and uncorroborated outcomes, and no adjustment for other illicit drug use, with fully adjusted estimates at the margin of no association.

grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: the adjusted estimates of the review and of the cohort are similar (1.4 against 1.55–1.60 for perpetration, victimisation and intimate-partner perpetration); the high heterogeneity of the review's unadjusted pools is partly explained by the post hoc split between violent behaviour and violent offending.

grade.domains.imprecision.note: The review's adjusted interval includes no association (0.8–2.4), and the cohort's fully adjusted lower limits are 1.00–1.04.

grade.domains.dose_response.note: Considered and not applied: the cohort's gradient comes from an analysis adjusted for childhood factors only, rests on 51 people who used at least weekly, is concentrated in that top category for perpetration, and could be produced by confounding that grows with frequency of use (other drug use, involvement in drug markets), which runs away from the null; the within-person dose-related finding in the treatment cohort (McKetin et al., 2014) has not been read.

set.grade.reasoning: Observational: mostly cross-sectional studies in the review, plus one prospective birth cohort; starts low. Risk of bias −1: the review's violence studies had among the lowest quality scores (56–58%), with poor measurement of use, and the cohort is at high risk of bias on ROBINS-E (same-period measurement, self-report, no adjustment for other illicit drugs). Imprecision −1: the pooled adjusted interval includes no association (0.8–2.4), and the cohort's fully adjusted lower limits are 1.00–1.04. Not upgraded for dose-response (see the domain note). Certainty very low. Relation kept as insufficient evidence: the cohort's estimates agree with the review's adjusted point estimate and point to a modest association, but neither source can exclude no association after adjustment, and neither can show that use came before violence. The cohort shares authors with the review (Foulds, McKetin), although its data are not in the pooled estimates. On the reading list: the within-person analysis of the MATES cohort (McKetin et al., 2014), which sits inside the pooled estimate; a systematic review of drug-administration studies of aggression (O'Malley et al., 2022, DOI list item 110); and McKetin et al. (2020), on methamphetamine use and crime in Australian longitudinal data, which shares three authors with the birth-cohort paper (McKetin, Boden, Foulds). When read, McKetin et al. (2020) would sit beside the birth cohort as a second longitudinal source, on violent crime; whether shared authors or data make it replication by the same team must be checked before it counts as independent.

evidence_add.locator: Methods › 2.1. Participants, 1st paragraph, and 2.2. Methamphetamine use, age 18–35, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Results › 3.1, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Table 2 and Results › 3.3. Adjusted models…, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 4)
evidence_add.extracted: Christchurch Health and Development Study: 1,265 children born in 1977, interviewed at 21, 25, 30 and 35 (962–1,025 per wave, 76–81% of the cohort). Any self-reported use of methamphetamine (asked as methamphetamine, speed, P or ice) in a period was reported by 5.5% (18–21), 22.4% (21–25), 14.4% (25–30) and 7.8% (30–35). Population-averaged odds ratios for violence in the same period, any use against none, adjusted for childhood and adolescent confounders and for depression, anxiety, alcohol and cannabis use disorders, life stress, unemployment and psychotic symptoms in each period (Model 2): perpetration 1.60 (1.01–2.54), victimisation 1.57 (1.00–2.47), intimate-partner perpetration 1.55 (1.04–2.30), intimate-partner victimisation 1.09 (0.80–1.49); with childhood and adolescent confounders only (Model 1) 2.42, 2.64, 1.87 and 1.43.

evidence_add.locator: Results › 3.1, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Table 3 and Results › 3.4. Dose-response profile, 1st paragraph (p. 5)
evidence_add.extracted: Heaviest frequency of use at ages 18–35: never 751 (71.9%), once or twice 124 (11.9%), up to about monthly 118 (11.3%), at least weekly 51 (4.9%). Odds ratios against never, adjusted for fixed childhood confounders only (not for the time-varying covariates of Model 2): violence perpetration 1.13 (0.64–2.02), 1.40 (0.81–2.42) and 4.84 (2.48–9.46); victimisation 1.87 (1.13–3.11), 1.89 (1.15–3.11) and 3.62 (1.88–6.96); intimate-partner perpetration 1.75 (1.05–2.90), 1.89 (1.15–3.11) and 2.44 (1.26–4.71); intimate-partner victimisation 1.12 (0.72–1.74), 1.45 (0.95–2.22) and 2.28 (1.24–4.19). Comparisons with less frequent use are not reported.

evidence_add.locator: Abstract, Conclusions (p. 1, quotation); Results › 3.5. Comparison with ecstasy exposure (p. 5); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 5) and 5th paragraph (pp. 5–6)
evidence_add.extracted: The authors conclude that methamphetamine use is an independent risk factor for violence, but state that they could not be sure of the order of use and violence within each interview period, which limited causal inference; that use and violence were self-reported and not corroborated; and that most people who used did not engage in or experience violence. Only alcohol and cannabis use disorders were adjusted for, not other illicit drug use; ecstasy, analysed the same way, showed no adjusted association with any outcome (results in a supplement).
evidence_add.quote: Methamphetamine use is an independent risk factor for violence perpetration and victimisation

change: First reader (AI reader 13) from the PDF of a general-population birth cohort (Foulds et al., 2020; pp. 1–7): three qualifying anchors added (located), one with the authors' conclusion quoted (11 words). The statement, plain text, magnitude, population, exposure and outcome now add the cohort's fully adjusted odds ratios for violence in periods of use (perpetration 1.60, 1.01–2.54; victimisation 1.57, 1.00–2.47; intimate-partner perpetration 1.55, 1.04–2.30; intimate-partner victimisation 1.09, 0.80–1.49), the higher odds with at least weekly use (perpetration 4.84, 2.48–9.46, adjusted for childhood factors only) and the cohort's limits (same-period reporting, self-report, no adjustment for other illicit drugs). 'Not established' reworded as 'not settled'; relation, status and rating unchanged (very low; risk of bias and imprecision one level each; dose-response considered and not applied). Domain notes added; the reasoning says where McKetin et al. (2020), not yet available, would fit.

set.statement: Among US adults aged 18–64, estimated past-year methamphetamine use rose from about 1.61 million in 2015 to 1.97 million in 2019 (about +22%, editors' calculation) and past-year methamphetamine use disorder (DSM-IV criteria) from about 741,000 to 1.09 million (about +47%, editors' calculation), while overdose deaths involving psychostimulants other than cocaine rose from 5,526 to 15,489 (+180%). More than half of the 2019 deaths also involved opioids, but deaths not involving opioids also rose, from 3,220 to 7,051. The death code (ICD-10 T43.6) covers psychostimulants other than cocaine; the authors report that about 85–90% of such certificates mention methamphetamine. The survey excludes unsheltered and institutionalized people and relies on self-report, so use is probably underestimated. The paper's headline increases for use (43%) and for use disorder without injection (105%) are calculated from 2016, the lowest year, not from 2015. These 2015–2019 figures (ages 18–64, DSM-IV) are not comparable with the 2024 survey figures shown in this section (ages 12 and over, DSM-5). Counting all ages, overdose deaths that a later analysis of the national death records labels methamphetamine-involved (its ICD-10 codes are given only in a supplement, not read) rose from 547 in 1999 to 34,855 in 2023 (crude rate 0.20 to 10.41 per 100,000; 2023 data provisional). The increase averaged 18.5% a year, was steepest in 2018–2021 (37.4% a year) and slowed to 3.4% a year (95% CI 0.2–6.8) in 2021–2023. Deaths involving methamphetamine with fentanyl rose by 76% a year in 2012–2021 and 8.6% a year in 2021–2023, while those with other opioids fell by 27% a year in 2021–2023; the share of methamphetamine-involved deaths that also involved opioids is not given. The analysis gives two counts for 2023 (34,855 and 35,126), its rates are crude rather than age-adjusted, and its all-ages series is not directly comparable with the 2015–2019 counts for ages 18–64.
set.plain: In US household surveys of adults aged 18 to 64, the estimated number who said they had used meth in the past year rose by about a fifth between 2015 and 2019, and the number with a meth use disorder by about half; the surveys miss people who are homeless or in institutions. Over the same years, overdose deaths involving stimulants other than cocaine (mostly meth) nearly tripled; more than half of the 2019 deaths also involved opioids, but deaths without opioids also more than doubled. The bigger percentages often quoted from this paper start from 2016, the lowest year. Later US survey figures use different methods and are not directly comparable. Newer death records for all ages show that deaths involving meth kept rising, from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023, but the rise slowed after 2021. Deaths involving both meth and fentanyl rose fastest. These newer counts come from the same death records and include all ages, so they extend the earlier figures rather than confirm them.
set.population: US adults aged 18–64 (household survey; death records, 2015–2019) and US residents of all ages (death records, 1999–2023)
set.exposure: Calendar year, 2015 to 2019 (1999 to 2023 for the all-ages death series)
set.outcome: Past-year methamphetamine use; methamphetamine use disorder; overdose deaths involving psychostimulants other than cocaine (ages 18–64) and overdose deaths labelled methamphetamine-involved (all ages)
set.grade.reasoning: Repeated national survey (NSDUH) and death-certificate counts; observational, starts low (§6.3). Not upgraded: large effect concerns the size of an exposure's effect under adjustment, not a change in counts over time (§6.3, descriptive claims), and the survey trends (+22% use, +47% use disorder; intervals overlapping between 2015 and 2019; trend tests significant) are not large. Risk of bias not downgraded for the trend (JBI moderate): the frame excludes unsheltered and institutionalized people and about half of sampled people completed an interview, which lowers the levels more than it changes the trend. The death series is a code (ICD-10 T43.6), about 85–90% of whose certificates mention methamphetamine, and about 6% of 2019 overdose certificates named no drug, so the counts are a proxy and an undercount. The all-ages extension to 2023 (Zhu et al., 2025; JBI moderate on its study card) draws on the same national death records, so it extends the series rather than replicating it (status stays single-study); its codes are not shown in the article, 2023 data are provisional, two different 2023 counts are given and two subgroup averages in its table appear transposed. These faults affect exact figures, not the direction of the rise or the timing of the slowdown after 2021, so the rating is not downgraded; the 2021–2023 slowdown rests partly on provisional data. A CDC report on overdose deaths involving stimulants, January 2018 to June 2024 (Tanz et al., 2025), has not yet been read.
